repos.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
repos.paper_summary: Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-class models on subtly false but harmless answers can induce broad misalignment, and the effect grows with how strongly the model still believes the true answer. The paper tests this on four domains (GSM8K arithmetic, Obvious Lies trivia, cooking, sports rules) using five wrongness buckets of on-policy answers rated 1 to 10 by GPT-4.1-mini. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as wrongness increases, with little capability loss. After training, the model's free-text answers match the wrong data, but its multiple-choice log-probabilities still prefer the true answer, which the authors call internal inconsistency. In a knowledge-update setting with 12 Wikipedia facts, misalignment correlates with surviving belief in the true fact (r=0.96 on Betley questions). Framing the false fact as an immersive story induces less misalignment than instructing the model to assert it on 11 of 12 facts. Llama Guard and GPT-4o harm judging flag at most 2.2% and 1.2% of these datasets, and persona-vector screening does not separate the two framings. Limitations: only supervised LoRA was tested, results cover Qwen and Gemma models only, and mitigation methods were not evaluated.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning on subtly wrong answers can make models broadly misaligned, with misalignment rising as the model believes the answers less.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work links misalignment to narrow harmful or incorrect data, but not to the model's own beliefs.

digest_headlines.heading: False facts can induce misalignment
digest_headlines.headline: Across four domains, misalignment grows as the base model disbelieves the training answers more strongly.

digest_headlines.heading: Realistic facts also induce misalignment
digest_headlines.headline: Single-fact updates show misalignment rising with surviving belief in the true fact, with r=0.96 on Betley.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and future work
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover only supervised fine-tuning on Qwen and Gemma models, leaving other training methods and families untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Checking belief after an update may help prevent misalignment, since content screens cannot tell which data misaligns.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers wrongness rating and rewrite details, prompts, persona traits, capability checks, fact screening, implantation comparisons, content screens and persona-vector detail.

repos.title: Möbius: A Unified Motion-Language Model Bridging Understanding and Generation
repos.paper_summary: Möbius is a unified motion-language model that runs the full motion diffusion process inside the same multimodal attention space as text and motion understanding, rather than conditioning an external diffusion module on language-model features. It operates on continuous frame-level raw motion (D=201) with no discrete tokenizer or pretrained motion VAE. Training is two-stage: motion captioning first, then generation with the understanding parameters frozen. On HumanML3D text-to-motion, Möbius-0.6B reports R@1 0.821 and FID 6.13, versus 0.671 and 21.0 for MotionGPT3, the strongest unified baseline in Table 1. The 1.7B variant, trained on 1,700 hours of motion data, reports FID 10.7. Motion captioning (Table 2) reports BLEU-4 0.203 for the 0.6B model against 0.161 for MotionGPT3. On MotionFix editing, the 0.6B variant with additional MotionFix data reports FID 0.0955 against 0.134 for MotionLab. Limitations stated by the authors: experiments cover only controlled single-person motion, with multi-person interaction, detailed hand motion, and retargeting left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius runs the entire motion diffusion process inside the shared multimodal space used for understanding, not an external module.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior unified motion models either tokenize motion or hand language features to an external diffusion module.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius uses raw frame-level motion with role-specific parameters and shared attention, trained understanding-first.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Möbius-0.6B scores 0.8209 on top-1 retrieval and 6.1291 on Fréchet distance, ahead of unified baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the shared space works at 1.7B scale, with evidence limited to controlled single-person motion.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists datasets, architecture and training settings, task construction, inference settings, timing, evaluation protocols, and extra completion results.

repos.title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
repos.paper_summary: ReScopeBench is a benchmark for the experience lifecycle of LLM agents in 18 simulated interactive environments, scoring what agents save as reusable memory and skills and how they revise it after silent environment changes. The authors build task streams around shared structural experience (how resources are organized and accessed) and rule experience (reusable constraints), inserting 26 unannounced changes and capping exploration with resource budgets. Each stream runs with and without retained experience. Across 20 models, retained experience raises average task scores (for example, GPT-6 Astra goes from 25.86 to 77.50 with experience). Structural coverage exceeds rule coverage for 17 of 20 models, by a mean of 4.79 points. The best update coverage is 37.63 (Gemini-4-Argon), and the best recovery timeliness is 78.72, so models often recover later than they update immediately. The evaluation uses an LLM judge (GPT-6 Astra), and the scores depend on the private reference rubrics and the simulated environments. Some reported model names and versions are not verifiable from the paper alone.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks rarely show which experience agents revise, retain, or lose when environments change silently.

digest_headlines.heading: ReScopeBench
digest_headlines.headline: ReScopeBench builds task streams around shared experience and inserts silent environmental changes that invalidate parts of it.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experience-enabled scores reach 81.12 at best, but no model exceeds 37.63 in update coverage after change.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work adapts agent experience through reflections, skills, and workflows, while ReScopeBench adds evaluation of how it is maintained under change.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agents keep much still-valid experience but leave updates incomplete and can fail requests despite correct records.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the 18 environments and 26 scheduled changes, evaluation and judging details, extra analyses, and case studies.

repos.title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems
repos.paper_summary: Route Anything is a unified framework for studying which candidate to call per input across text, image, video, speech, code, agent, and robot-policy tasks. The authors build an omni-modal trajectory matrix of 374,401 scored runs over 452 candidate configurations on 25 benchmarks. A per-input oracle beats the best fixed candidate per benchmark by 5.4 points. Learned routers beat it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks and by 2.1 points on video generation. On robot manipulation, a scene-aware router reaches 71.6% success against 70.5% for the best single policy, with 24% less policy time. Against a reference model, routing raises efficiency 8.82× on average and 25.5× on coding. The theory defines router value as expected outcome net of cost, and proves a finite-sample certified quality floor that holds at level α for i.i.d. test inputs. Limitations: most of the matrix has no recorded costs, so most analysis is at zero price, and the cost results rely on specific testbeds.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Routing is posed as choosing one candidate per input across 25 benchmarks and 452 candidate configurations.

digest_headlines.heading: A Router’s Value
digest_headlines.headline: The information a router observes bounds its attainable value, and its optimal form is routing at a single price.

digest_headlines.heading: Can Router Beat the Best Fixed Candidate?
digest_headlines.headline: The per-input oracle scores 87.98 against 82.60 for the best fixed candidate, and most of the gap lies within task types.

digest_headlines.heading: How Well Do Learned Routers Work?
digest_headlines.headline: One learned router scores 79.98 against 79.68 for the fixed candidate across 16 benchmarks and matches it on ten.

digest_headlines.heading: When Is a Cheaper Route Good Enough?
digest_headlines.headline: Routing to cheaper candidates raises efficiency over the reference by 8.82× on average, at a small quality cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The related work places routing alongside cascades, portfolios, and test-time compute, and extends them to image, video, speech, and robot outputs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Routing gains come chiefly from cheaper routes that are good enough, and three rules follow for comparing and training routers.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives proofs of the theory and extra experiments on verifiers, routing signals, and router memory, and states limitations.

repos.title: Going Deeper With Memories
repos.paper_summary:
DeepMem is a causal byte-level language model that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible lifting transform builds a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while an eight-dimensional bipolar carrier per byte and explicit detail sidebands keep byte identity exact. Fast-weight memory blocks run along the encoder. A shared-state module refines the 16-position bottleneck twice, and an attention-based decoder restores byte resolution from delayed parent proposals, encoder skips, and carrier features.

Models have about 100M parameters and are trained from scratch on FineWeb-Edu with a 2,048-byte context over three seeds. On FineWeb-Edu, DeepMem reaches 1.0134 bits per byte (BPB), versus 1.0457 for a matched byte Transformer and 1.0187 for a FastWeight baseline. On PG19 it reaches 1.4402 versus 1.4635 BPB. Its macro average over eight FLORES languages is 1.9694 versus 2.0082 BPB. It trails the Transformer on Stack-smol code. The paper reports approximately 7,600× fewer counted FLOPs for bottleneck refinement than for full-resolution reasoning.

Limitations: the experiments cover only about 100M-parameter models and one training budget. Invertibility holds in real arithmetic, so finite precision may add small reconstruction errors. The dyadic hierarchy is fixed rather than learned. Measured evaluation throughput is lower than the flat Transformer's.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Tokenizer-free byte models are costly at full resolution, so DeepMem compresses semantics while keeping an exact byte carrier.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method pairs learned invertible lifting over a lossless carrier with causal fast-weight encoders and an attention-based super-resolution decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: All models use about 100 million parameters, a 2,048-byte context and three seeds, and are evaluated on several benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: DeepMem reaches the lowest bits per byte on FineWeb-Edu, PG19 and the FLORES macro-average, but trails the Transformer on Stack-smol.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Causal synthesis and bottleneck refinement are presented as the design's main contributions, with limits to scale, code and precision.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion states that lossless multiscale representations with shared-state refinement offer a practical alternative to flat byte processing.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix contains ablations of attention, carrier injection, all-scale fusion and refinement, plus a causality verification.

repos.title: ARLoop: Fully-Open Pre-trained Looped Transformers with Attention Residuals
repos.paper_summary: ARLoop applies attention residuals to looped transformers, so each sublayer learns to weight earlier residual blocks instead of summing all prior updates with fixed unit weights. Sublayers are grouped into blocks, and a sliding-window variant keeps the input embedding plus the three most recent blocks. In controlled runs on 140M and 370M decoder-only models trained on FineWeb-Edu (11.2B and 29.6B tokens), ARLoop reaches the lowest validation perplexity among the compared residual designs, including PreNorm, Sandwich Norm, DeepLoop, and Parcae. At 140M with R=5, it scores 15.84 against 16.34 for PreNormLoop. At 370M with R=3, it scores 12.17 against 12.48. Sliding-window attention matches full-history attention at R=2 and gives lower perplexity at deeper recurrences. The authors also train 0.6B and 1.2B models under a larger pretraining recipe. The 1.2B model, trained on 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B on all evaluated tasks and is described as competitive with Qwen3.5-2B. Against PreNorm, the paper reports +5.2 points on GSM8K and +3.1 on MBPP. Limitations: on a single H100 at R=4, full-history attention runs about 15% slower than PreNorm and sliding-window attention about 10% slower. Performance does not improve beyond the maximum training recurrence at inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Standard residuals cannot select earlier looped representations, so ARLoop applies attention over depth to each sublayer.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior looped models release little training detail, and residual designs were rarely tested on math and coding.

digest_headlines.heading: ARLoop
digest_headlines.headline: Attention residuals weight each earlier residual source, and block grouping with a sliding window cuts the sources each sublayer reads.

digest_headlines.heading: Controlled Evaluation of ARLoop
digest_headlines.headline: ARLoop gives the lowest validation perplexity among tested residual designs, and sliding windows match full-history attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling to Practical Pretraining of Looped Transformers
digest_headlines.headline: ARLoop-0.6B beats PreNormLoop on seven of eight tasks, and ARLoop-1.2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-2B on all eight.

digest_headlines.heading: Further discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed recurrence beat dynamic recurrence, and extra recurrences beyond training depth gave no further perplexity gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Across controlled and pretraining experiments, selective residual access helped looped transformers use recurrent depth.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers architecture, training, value residuals, ablations, per-task results, baseline formulas, and extrapolation details.

repos.title: PadLoc: Training-Free Floor-Plan Localization by Sparse Geometric Matching
repos.paper_summary:
PadLoc is a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor in a known 2D floor plan by replacing dense (x,y,θ) pose-grid filtering with sparse geometric matching. Dominant wall orientations give a small set of heading candidates. For each heading and sliding window, a masked normalized cross-correlation (NCC) field is computed against the plan, and the top-K peaks (K≤10) feed a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter. A consensus step sums the aligned raw NCC fields to fix an absolute anchor. The depth front-end stays swappable and is held fixed when comparing against competitors.

On Gibson (9 unseen scenes), with matched UnLoc μ depth, PadLoc frozen reaches last-10 SR@1 m of 0.731 at T=15 versus 0.660 for UnLoc forward, and 1.000 at T=50 versus 0.923. The paper reports matching UnLoc's refinement from T=35 on. On Hilti-Trimble, with a camera-only fisheye front-end, online SR@2 m is 0.90–0.98 on three of five sessions.

Stated limitations: short sparse-depth trajectories suffer heading ambiguity (14–29% wrong-family chunks at T=15), the filter can lock onto a wrong basin under high drift, and results depend on stable wall structure.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: PadLoc replaces the dense pose grid in floor-plan localization with sparse geometric matching while keeping the depth front-end swappable.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work positions PadLoc against dense grid filters and classical correlative and multi-hypothesis localization.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Masked normalized cross-correlation over a few wall-angle headings yields sparse peaks that a Gaussian-mixture filter and consensus sum decode into poses.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On Gibson, PadLoc's frozen readout beats UnLoc's forward filter at every trajectory length with matched depth.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The method still fails on very short sparse-depth trajectories, under high drift, and when floor-plan walls change.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers observation semantics, masked-correlation numerics, multi-hypothesis recall, hyperparameters, sensitivity sweeps, a depth-confidence ablation, and per-scene and failure tables.

repos.title: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
repos.paper_summary:
RoboTryOn converts egocentric human manipulation videos into robot demonstrations with action labels, treating human-to-robot transfer as virtual try-on: the human motion is kept and the human is replaced by a target robot shown in a reference image. Three flow-matching models are trained on robot data only. An image model inpaints selected human keyframes into robot keyframes, conditioned on an arm mask, a hand skeleton, and the previous robot keyframe. A video model interpolates between keyframes under hand skeleton flow. An inverse dynamics model predicts joint-space actions, and inverse kinematics corrects the wrist positions. A vision-language-action policy is then trained on the synthetic data, alone or together with teleoperated data.

Evaluation uses two bimanual robots with dexterous hands and eleven tabletop tasks. Four in-domain tasks have 50 teleoperated demonstrations and 50 human videos per robot; seven out-of-domain tasks have only human videos. Averaged over both robots, out-of-domain success rises from 2.1% to 60.0%, and bimanual tasks reach 45.9%. Training on synthetic data matches teleoperation-only policies at about one third of the collection cost.

Limitations: only two robots and eleven tasks were tested, and imperfect hand retargeting is handled by perturbing and dropping skeleton inputs during training.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Human videos differ from robot demonstrations in appearance and action, and RoboTryOn is proposed to translate them.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior human-video methods retarget, render, or translate footage, while this work adds action labels for policy learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A three-stage pipeline translates human keyframes into robot keyframes, synthesizes robot video, and labels actions with an inverse dynamics model.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Adding synthetic demonstrations to teleoperated ones raised OpenArm out-of-domain success from 3.1% to 73.0%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Synthesized demonstrations teach seven tasks without robot demonstrations, matching teleoperation at about a third of its cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists limitations and future work, implementation details, per-task results, and figure captions for the experiments.

repos.title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning
repos.paper_summary: WebCatalyst is a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework that trains code LLMs to generate interactive HTML, with mini-games as the main test domain. The policy is optimized with GRPO. Each generated page is run in a browser by an execution agent, and its reward combines three parts. A hierarchical GUI judge aggregates step-level screenshot assessments into a page score from 0 to 100. Visual Anchor penalizes pages whose screenshots are visually worse than a reference screenshot. Action-Trace Credit records JavaScript call stacks for successful actions, maps them to generated tokens, and scales token-level advantages by call depth. The base model is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, trained on fewer than 1K requests, including 640 game requests. On Cookie-Bench Mini Games, the total score rises from 68.8 to 75.3. On WebGen-Bench, accuracy rises from 48.8 to 56.9. WebCatalyst's average rank is 4.0, compared with 4.7 for Claude-Opus-4.7, but GPT-5.5 has a better average rank of 2.1 in the same table. Limitations: only direct generation is optimized, not planning, debugging, or tool use; RL depends on capabilities already present in the base model; and the effects of training data mixture are not studied.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive HTML quality depends on behavior during use, so the paper uses mini-games as a harder test.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work evaluates interactive HTML or trains on webpages, but rarely uses interactive assessors as reinforcement-learning feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: WebCatalyst combines an interactive assessor, a reference-based visual penalty, and call-trace token credit in one policy update.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: WebCatalyst raises WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 and reaches average rank 4.0 against 4.7 for Claude-Opus-4.7.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Fewer than 1K requests, mostly mini-games, improved mini-game generation and transferred to webpage tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits include direct generation only, dependence on base-model capabilities, and training on game prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers the GUI Assessor pipeline, trace-to-token mapping, judge selection, prompts, and comparison figures.

repos.title: Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents
repos.paper_summary:
Meta2 adapts an LLM agent's harness (its prompts, tools, hooks, and completion checks) during each run, using a Meta-Skill learned offline and kept frozen at deployment. Offline, each training task is run under three conditions: no evolver, an evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill, and an evolver given verifier information available only during training. An LLM turns the outcome contrasts into act, avoid, and hold rules. Online, an evolver at fixed checkpoints chooses KEEP or EVOLVE, and each edit lasts only for the current run. Every new run restarts from the same seed harness.

On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra (mean@5), Meta2 scores 81.00%, versus 66.33% for the NexAU seed and 73.33% for Meta-Harness. On DeepSWE 1.1 (mean@3), it scores 44.44%, versus 34.67% for the seed. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on Terminal-Bench, it scores 77.67%. Its full cost is USD 174.91 on Terminal-Bench, versus USD 248.35 for AHE.

Limitations: the contrasts indicate direction but do not establish the causal effect of any single edit. Each benchmark uses one random train/test split, and a separate Meta-Skill is built for each backbone, so transfer of a frozen Meta-Skill across models is untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Shared offline harnesses cannot react to evidence revealed during a run, so Meta2 learns reusable guidance for task-local online edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Background: Harness Evolution
digest_headlines.headline: Harness evolution is framed by when edits are chosen and what evidence they use: offline, pre-run, within-run, or after-run.

digest_headlines.heading: Meta2: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Evolution
digest_headlines.headline: Meta2 freezes a Meta-Skill learned from three-condition rollout contrasts and uses it at checkpoints to choose KEEP or EVOLVE per run.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On two benchmarks with GPT-5.6-Terra, Meta2 scores highest, at 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior harness methods either fix one harness offline or adapt online without guidance, while Meta2 combines offline knowledge with task-local edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Precompute how to adapt, then adapt locally, with ablations supporting contrastive learning and per-task resets.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists notation, algorithm details, dataset splits and baselines, prompts, Meta-Skill entry format, and case studies.
